explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. The daughters of Moab invited the men to the sacrifices for their gods (Numbers 25:2). An invitation can sound small, but look where this one led. The people ate and bowed down to those gods, and that's where the chapter turns heavier.

A sheep-shearing feast is a real kind of gathering in Scripture, but it isn't the one in this verse. The invitation was to the sacrifices for their gods (Numbers 25:2). I think it matters what kind of invitation it was, because it led straight to eating and bowing down to those gods.

A wedding feast would be a happy thing, and that's why this one sticks out. The verse says the women invited the men to the sacrifices for their gods (Numbers 25:2). Nothing in the verse mentions a wedding. What follows is that the people ate and bowed down to these gods.

I get why it might sound that way, but the text says more. Verse 2 says, "And the people ate and bowed down to these gods." So they did more than stand at the edge of the crowd. They took part, and verse 3 says Israel joined in worshiping Baal of Peor.

That's right, baker. The text says, "And the people ate and bowed down to these gods." (Numbers 25:2). They didn't just watch. They took part, and verse 3 says Israel joined in worshiping Baal of Peor.

Yes, friend. The text says, "…the anger of the LORD burned against them." (Numbers 25:3). Worshiping a false god was a serious matter. This is what the LORD's response looks like, and everything after it in the chapter follows from it.

explanations.answer: He waits to see what they do
explanations.explanation: I can see why that could sound calmer, but it isn't what the verse says. The verse says the anger of the LORD burned against them (Numbers 25:3). In the very next verse He is already speaking to Moses. The LORD is not waiting around here.

explanations.answer: He sends Moab out of the land
explanations.explanation: This verse turns toward Israel, not Moab. It says the anger of the LORD burned against them, meaning Israel, after they joined in worshiping Baal of Peor (Numbers 25:3). Nothing in the passage says He sent Moab out of any land. The anger is where the verse stays.

explanations.answer: So His fierce anger may turn away from Israel
explanations.explanation: That's the reason the LORD gives. He says it plainly: "…so that His fierce anger may turn away from Israel." (Numbers 25:4). It's a heavy command, and I think it's one to read slowly. The text gives us the reason, and we can stay right there with it.

explanations.answer: So Moab will see it and be afraid of Israel
explanations.explanation: That's a reason I could make up, but the text doesn't give it. The LORD gives His own reason: "…so that His fierce anger may turn away from Israel." (Numbers 25:4). Moab being afraid never comes up in the verse. Whenever we can, we let the text tell us the why.

explanations.answer: So the leaders cannot run off to join Moab
explanations.explanation: The verse never mentions leaders running off, so nothing in it points that way. What it says is that the order is given "…so that His fierce anger may turn away from Israel." (Numbers 25:4). The LORD's anger is the reason, and the verse leaves it there. This is a hard verse, and it's best read just as it's written.
That's right. Moses told "the judges of Israel" (Numbers 25:5). They're the ones he gives the order to. It's a short verse, but the people it names are right there in the text.

Priests do show up later in this chapter, but not here. Moses gives this order to the judges of Israel (Numbers 25:5). Phinehas, Aaron the priest's grandson, doesn't step in until verse 7. So the judges are the ones Moses speaks to in this verse.

I can see why you'd think soldiers, since the order is a hard one. But the verse says Moses told the judges of Israel (Numbers 25:5). Soldiers aren't mentioned in it at all. I'd read it twice before picking a word it doesn't use.

Yes, friend. The text says this happened "…in the sight of Moses and the whole congregation of Israel while they were weeping at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting." (Numbers 25:6). So the whole community was already weeping when this happened. I think that tells us how heavy the moment was.

This one is true, and the text says so right out. The man came "…in the sight of Moses and the whole congregation of Israel while they were weeping at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting." (Numbers 25:6). They were weeping at the Tent of Meeting when it happened. I think it was a hard day for everyone there.

explanations.answer: The plague against them is halted
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Verse 8 says, "So the plague against the Israelites was halted…" (Numbers 25:8). It happens right after Phinehas acts. Verse 9 then tells us the cost of the plague, and it's a heavy number.

No army shows up in these verses. The text says the plague against the Israelites was halted (Numbers 25:8). Moab's army is never mentioned in this passage at all. What changes right after Phinehas acts is the plague.

explanations.answer: They break camp and leave Shittim
explanations.explanation: Packing up is a fair guess. The text, though, says the plague against the Israelites was halted (Numbers 25:8). It doesn't say they moved anywhere. The halt is what happens next.
That's right. Verse 9 says, "…those who died in the plague numbered 24,000." This is one of the heaviest parts of the chapter. It's a number we should read slowly and quietly.

That number is too low, friend. Verse 9 says, "…those who died in the plague numbered 24,000." It's easy to mix up numbers like these, and I do it with my own cookie counts all the time. This is a heavy verse, so I'd read it slowly.
That number is much too low. The text says, "…those who died in the plague numbered 24,000." (Numbers 25:9). It's a heavy verse, and the real number is the one it gives. I'd read it slowly.

explanations.answer: He was zealous for the LORD's sake
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The LORD says Phinehas "…was zealous for My sake among them, so that I did not consume the Israelites in My zeal." (Numbers 25:11). That's the reason the LORD gives for Phinehas. The text tells us the why, so we can simply take it as it's written.

explanations.answer: He was merciful to the guilty man
explanations.explanation: The LORD doesn't say that here. He says Phinehas "…was zealous for My sake among them…" (Numbers 25:11). Nothing in the passage describes Phinehas as merciful to the man. Zeal is the word the LORD uses.

explanations.answer: He was humble before the assembly
explanations.explanation: The text does say Phinehas got up from the assembly (Numbers 25:7). But the LORD's reason is different: Phinehas "…was zealous for My sake among them…" (Numbers 25:11). Humility isn't the word the LORD uses. When the LORD gives a reason, that's the one to go with.

explanations.answer: The LORD is granting him His covenant of peace
explanations.explanation: That's right. The LORD says, "Declare, therefore, that I am granting him My covenant of peace." (Numbers 25:12). It's a gift from the LORD to Phinehas. I think it's a good word to land on after such a heavy chapter.

explanations.answer: He will lead Israel after Moses is gone
explanations.explanation: Leading Israel is a big job, but this verse doesn't give it to Phinehas. The LORD tells Moses to declare that He is granting Phinehas His covenant of peace (Numbers 25:12). Nothing here says Phinehas will lead after Moses. The covenant of peace is the gift in this verse.

explanations.answer: He will be given a city of his own
explanations.explanation: A city of his own would be nice, but this verse doesn't say it. The LORD says, "Declare, therefore, that I am granting him My covenant of peace." (Numbers 25:12). The gift is a covenant, and no city is named here. Good guess for a baker who likes things with a front door, though.

That's right, baker. The LORD says, "It will be a covenant of permanent priesthood for him and his descendants…" (Numbers 25:13). Permanent is a strong word. The gift reaches past Phinehas to his descendants too.

It's actually true. The LORD says, "It will be a covenant of permanent priesthood for him and his descendants…" (Numbers 25:13). The word is permanent, and it includes his descendants. So the text says exactly what the card says.

Yes, friend. The LORD says Phinehas "…was zealous for his God and made atonement for the Israelites." (Numbers 25:13). That's the second thing the LORD says about him. The text gives it in just those words.

An altar is a thing a priest's family might know about, but this verse doesn't mention one. The LORD says Phinehas "…was zealous for his God and made atonement for the Israelites." (Numbers 25:13). Atonement is the word to remember. No altar is built in this passage.

Prayer is a good thing to do, but it isn't what this verse says. The LORD says Phinehas "…was zealous for his God and made atonement for the Israelites." (Numbers 25:13). Nothing in this passage has Phinehas leading a prayer. Atonement is what the LORD names.

That's right, baker. Verse 15 says Cozbi was "…the daughter of Zur, a tribal chief of a Midianite family." So Zur was a leader among the Midianites. Cozbi gets her name here, and I think that matters.

Balak was king of Moab (Numbers 22:4), and this woman was Midianite. Verse 15 says Cozbi was the daughter of Zur, a tribal chief of a Midianite family. Moab and Midian are different peoples in this chapter. Balak is a name from nearby, but he isn't her father here.

Jethro was Moses' father-in-law and the priest of Midian (Exodus 3:1), so I see why the name came to mind. But Numbers 25:15 says Cozbi was the daughter of Zur, a tribal chief of a Midianite family. Jethro isn't named in this passage. Zur is the name the text gives.

explanations.answer: They deceived Israel in the matter of Peor
explanations.explanation: That's it. The LORD says, "For they assailed you deceitfully when they seduced you in the matter of Peor…" (Numbers 25:18). That's the reason He gives for the order. It ties back to the very beginning of the chapter.

explanations.answer: They blocked Israel's road into Canaan
explanations.explanation: That sounds like a believable reason, but it's not the one the LORD gives. He says, "For they assailed you deceitfully when they seduced you in the matter of Peor…" (Numbers 25:18). Nothing in this passage mentions a blocked road. The reason is what happened at Peor.

explanations.answer: They raided Israel's camp in the night
explanations.explanation: A night raid would make a dramatic reason, but the text doesn't say that. The LORD says, "For they assailed you deceitfully when they seduced you in the matter of Peor…" (Numbers 25:18). The word is deceitfully, and it's about Peor. No raid is mentioned in this passage.
